implementation_notes: The .NET stack provides the structure: ObjectPool<T>.Get()/Return() with a PooledObjectPolicy<T> that creates instances and resets them on return (or IResettable.TryReset on the pooled type), normally registered in dependency injection through ObjectPoolProvider; all members are thread-safe. For arrays there is a cheaper, array-shaped realisation in System.Buffers.ArrayPool<T>.Shared.Rent(length)/Return(array), which recycles buckets of buffers instead of individual objects. A hand-written pool is only justified when instances must be validated before being handed out (Return has no validation hook) or when the pool must expose application-specific lease semantics.
pitfalls: ObjectPool<T> bounds what it retains, not what it allocates: a burst can allocate far beyond the retention cap and the excess is simply left to the GC.
Return() trusts the caller - state the policy does not reset silently leaks into the next borrower, and a non-IDisposable pooled type with stale references keeps them alive.

After the pool is disposed, Get() throws ObjectDisposedException while Return() disposes the item, so shutdown order in DI hosts matters; ArrayPool buffers are also not zeroed and may contain the previous borrower's data.
